21-035.r: Limestone → calcium carbonate (CaCO3), as calcite and aragonite; in iron extraction it binds silica impurities.

21-036.r: Cement → main raw materials limestone, silica clay, marl; lime about 60–65% of weight, silica 17–25%; heated to 1,450 °C in a kiln. More than one option fits.

21-037.r: Cement sector → about 5–8% of global CO2 emissions; silica clay is mixed with limestone; limestone becomes lime in clinker production. II and III true, only one explains I.

21-038.r: Plaster of Paris → calcium sulphate hemihydrate (CaSO4·½H2O), made by heating (calcining) gypsum; used for casts on broken bones.
21-038.h: Gypsum holds 2 waters; Plaster of Paris keeps only half.

21-043.r: Gypsum → calcium sulphate dihydrate (CaSO4·2H2O), contains calcium; used as fertilizer, plaster, chalk, drywall.
21-043.t: Corundum is aluminium oxide and talc is magnesium silicate: no calcium.

21-044.r: Monazite → ore of thorium (also lanthanum, cerium); rich in Indian coastal beach sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh.

21-045.r: Mica → good conductor of heat but bad conductor of electricity; used as raw material in the electrical industry.

21-047.r: Best heat conductor among mercury, water, ether, benzene → mercury, a liquid metal; used in thermometers (about −40 to 356°C).

21-048.r: Poorest heat conductor among copper, lead, mercury, zinc → mercury (about 8.31 W/mK; lead 34.7 W/mK).

21-049.r: Mercury (quicksilver) → only common metal that is liquid at room temperature.

21-050.r: Liquid at room temperature (298 K or 25°C) → bromine and mercury; francium, caesium, gallium, rubidium melt just above it. Among the options → francium.

21-051.r: Mercury in thermometers → expands evenly with temperature ('high circulation power'), is shiny and easy to read, does not wet glass, conducts heat.

21-052.r: No reaction with water at all → lead, copper, silver, gold, platinum. Magnesium reacts with hot water; aluminium, iron, zinc react only with steam.

21-054.r: Iron is obtained from haematite (Fe2O3, about 69.9% Fe) and magnetite (Fe3O4, about 72.4% Fe).

21-055.r: Bailadila (Dantewada district, Chhattisgarh) → very high-grade haematite iron ore; first mapped by P.N. Bose (1898–1900).

21-056.r: Rusting → iron's weight increases, as iron combines with oxygen (with moisture) to form iron oxide.

21-058.r: Rust → iron oxide formed by iron, oxygen and moisture, not tannin (a plant substance used in tanning leather). A true, R false.

21-059.r: Galvanised iron → iron or steel coated with zinc; zinc oxidises first and shields the iron from rust. A and R true, R explains A.

21-063.r: Oil is not stored in galvanised (zinc-coated) iron → zinc reacts with fatty acids and moisture, forming toxic compounds, speeding rancidity and corrosion. All of above.

21-064.r: Corrosion (rusting) of iron → needs both oxygen and moisture; final product is hydrated iron (III) oxide, i.e. rust.

21-065.r: Silver articles turn black in air → tarnishing: silver reacts with sulphur compounds (H2S) to form a black silver sulphide (Ag2S) coat. Both statements true.

21-066.r: Brass utensils are coated with tin (Sn, atomic number 50) to prevent copper contamination.

21-067.r: Anodising aluminium → electrochemical deposition of an aluminium oxide layer, making the surface durable and rust-resistant.

21-068.r: More negative standard electrode potential → stronger reducing agent: B (–3 V) > C (–1.2 V) > A (0.5 V).

21-069.r: Sodium → easily cut with a knife; Mercury → liquid at room temperature; Silver → good conductor of electricity; Lead → poor conductor of heat.

21-070.r: Silver → best conductor of heat and electricity; Aluminium → metal found in highest amount; Gold → most flexible (malleable) metal; Lead → least heat-conducting.

21-072.r: Aluminium → produced mainly from bauxite (hydrated aluminium oxides: gibbsite, boehmite, diaspore); bauxite named after Les Baux village, southern France.

21-078.r: Corundum (Al2O3) and cryolite (Na3AlF6) → ores of aluminium, with bauxite and diaspore. Aluminium is third most abundant in the crust, after oxygen and silicon.

21-079.r: Correct statement (book): calcium carbonate is an abrasive ingredient of toothpaste, used only in opaque pastes as it is insoluble.
21-079.c: Both (a) and (b) are true: liquid sodium cools fast breeder reactors (the book itself names the FBTR), and calcium carbonate is a toothpaste abrasive. The book keeps (b).

21-080.r: Cracking → petroleum; Smelting → copper; Hydrogenation → edible fats; Vulcanisation → rubber.

21-081.r: Diamond → carbon; Marble → calcium (calcium carbonate); Sand → silicon (silicon dioxide, quartz); Ruby → aluminium.

21-082.r: Cinnabar → ore of mercury, not copper (copper → cuprite). Correct: aluminium – bauxite; zinc – calamine; iron – haematite.

21-083.r: Metals lighter than water (1 g/cm³) → lithium 0.53, potassium 0.862, sodium 0.971 g/cm³.

21-084.r: Decreasing density: gold (19.3) > mercury (13.6) > steel (7.8 g/cm³).

21-085.r: Melting point: boron 2453 K > iron 1808 K > silicon 1693 K > aluminium 933 K; boron is highest.

22-001.r: Copper → a pure metal, not an alloy; steel, brass and bronze are alloys.

22-002.r: Aeroplanes and train compartments → aluminium alloys (e.g. duralumin): low density, strength, easy shaping, corrosion resistance.

22-003.r: Amalgam → alloy of mercury with another metal; almost all metals form amalgams except iron.

22-005.r: Amalgam → mercury + another metal, so Mercury – Zinc is an amalgam.

22-006.r: Solder → tin + lead (about 32% tin, 68% lead); low melting point, good for heat-sensitive parts.

22-007.r: Bronze → copper + tin (most modern bronze about 88% copper, 12% tin).
22-007.t: Brass is copper + zinc; bronze is copper + tin.

22-009.r: German silver → nickel (alloy of copper, zinc, nickel; 0% silver, no aluminium); Solder → tin; Bleaching powder → chlorine (calcium hypochlorite); Hypo → sodium (sodium thiosulphate).

22-013.r: Copper share: bronze about 88% (highest), gunmetal 85%, brass 68–71% (rest zinc), German silver about 50%. Copper is common to brass, bronze and German silver.

22-019.r: True: brass = copper + zinc; amalgams mainly involve mercury. False: magnetite is an iron ore, not aluminium; photography uses silver bromide, not potassium nitrate.

22-020.r: Brass loses its colour (fades) in air → due to hydrogen sulphide.

22-021.r: Nickel added to stainless steel → makes it non-magnetic; extra carbon → more hardness.

22-022.r: Steel is made harder by increasing carbon; carbon distorts iron's crystal lattice and hardens it.

22-023.r: Steel slag (by-product of steel making; 16–25% iron, with calcium, silicon) → usable for road base, improving farm soil, and cement (up to 10% of clinker mix). All three.

22-024.r: Chromium added to iron → stainless steel that resists corrosion, rust and high temperature, with high hardness.

22-026.r: Stainless steel ≈ iron 89.4%, chromium 10.0%, manganese 0.35%, carbon 0.25% (plus a little nickel); silicon is not used. Chromium is the key metal.

22-032.r: Steel → iron + carbon, with up to 2% carbon (option 0.1–2%).

23-001.r: Carbon → forms the maximum number of compounds among the elements.

23-002.r: Diamond (relative density 3.5) and graphite (2.25) are carbon allotropes; coal is carbon-rich fuel. All contain carbon, so 'None of these'.

23-004.r: Thermodynamically most stable form of carbon → graphite (layers of graphene sheets, weakly bonded).

23-005.r: Graphite and diamond → both pure carbon, so they undergo the same chemical reactions; they differ in crystal structure (tetrahedral vs layered), hardness, conductivity.

23-007.r: Lab-grown diamonds → graphite as seed/carbon source under very high temperature and pressure (catalysts: chromium, iron, platinum). White sapphire (aluminium oxide) cannot form diamond.

23-009.r: First synthesis order: Kevlar (1965, Stephanie Kwolek, DuPont) → Fullerene (1985) → Graphene (2004, Geim and Novoselov) → Black gold.

23-010.r: Graphene → only carbon: a single layer of carbon atoms in a two-dimensional hexagonal lattice; basic unit of graphite, charcoal, carbon nanotubes, fullerenes.

23-012.r: Oxocarbon → compound of carbon and oxygen only, not an allotrope of carbon. Allotropes: diamond, graphite, fullerenes.

23-013.r: Pencil 'lead' → graphite mixed with a clay binder.
23-013.t: Pencils contain no lead metal; it is graphite.

23-015.r: Carbon fibres (90% or more carbon, made from PAN) → used in automobile and aircraft parts; they can be recycled, so statement 2 is wrong.

23-016.r: Fullerenes (third carbon allotrope) → 1996 Chemistry Nobel to Robert Curl, Harold Kroto, Richard Smalley; named after architect Buckminster Fuller. 'Faimen' was not in the team.

23-017.r: Fullerene → carbon allotrope, not a fluorine compound. Buckminsterfullerene C60: 60 carbon atoms, 12 pentagonal + 20 hexagonal faces, soccer-ball shape.
23-017.t: Teflon is the fluorine-containing polymer, not fullerene.

23-019.r: Wrong pair: Fullerene – fluorine organic compounds (it is a carbon allotrope). Correct: dry ice – solid CO2; keratin – protein of outer skin; mustard gas – chemical weapon.

23-021.r: Wrong pair: Fullerene – fluorine polymer (fullerene is a hollow carbon allotrope). Correct: Pyrene – fire extinguisher; sulfur dioxide – acid rain; Freon – refrigerant.

23-022.r: Sand → no carbon. Diamond, graphite (carbon allotropes) and coal (about 40–90% carbon) contain carbon.

23-023.r: Lignite (a coal) → contains carbon. Carbon content: lignite 25–35%, sub-bituminous 35–45%, bituminous 45–86%, anthracite 86–97% (highest).
23-023.h: L-S-B-A: Lignite lowest, Anthracite highest carbon.

23-025.r: Highest carbon → pig iron (3.5–4.5%); carbon steel 0.2–1.5%; alloy steel 0.1–1%; wrought iron below 0.08%.

23-026.r: Exam answer: sulfur (c). In fact sulfur also forms crystals (rhombic, monoclinic); diamond, quartz, graphite, salt, sugar and ice are crystalline.
23-026.c: Sulfur does form crystals (rhombic and monoclinic sulfur); (c) is only the expected exam answer.

23-027.r: Glass can be etched or scratched by diamond (abrasive, cuts glass) and hydrofluoric acid (HF, used for glass etching); not by aqua regia or concentrated sulfuric acid.

23-028.r: Carat (unit for weighing gems and pearls) → 200 mg.
23-028.t: Gem carat is a mass unit; gold carat measures purity.

23-029.r: Graphene → two-dimensional carbon (not silicon), excellent electrical conductor, thinnest yet strongest material; used as conducting electrodes in touchscreens, LCDs, OLEDs. Isolated 2004 by Geim, Novoselov.

23-031.r: True: calcium sulphate makes water hard; diamond is harder than copper and iron. False: air is mainly nitrogen (about 78%), not oxygen; vanaspati ghee uses hydrogenation, not nitrogen.

23-032.r: Lubricant for heavy machines → graphite: black, anti-seize, anti-friction carbon allotrope (graphite grease).

23-033.r: Graphite → used as a lubricant: hexagonal carbon layers held by weak van der Waals forces slide over each other.

23-034.r: Dry ice → solid (frozen) carbon dioxide, CO2, also called dry snow.
23-034.t: Not solid carbon monoxide and not frozen water.

23-039.r: Water gas → carbon monoxide + hydrogen (CO + H2), a synthesis gas; makes methyl alcohol: CO + 2H2 → CH3OH.

23-040.r: Gas escaping from a soda water bottle → carbon dioxide, dissolved under pressure to make the drink fizzy.

23-041.r: Bond order of CO → 3. Bond order = ½ × (bonding − antibonding electrons); CO has 10 valence electrons (four from carbon, six from oxygen).

24-001.r: Element with four electrons in its outermost orbit (valency four) → hydride formula XH4.

24-002.r: Hydrogen in water (H2O) by mass → 2/18 = 11.11%; molar mass of water = 2 + 16 = 18 g/mol.

24-003.r: 1 mole H2 = 2 g gives 290 kJ; 4 g = 2 moles → 290 × 2 = 580 kJ.

24-004.r: Burning hydrogen (with oxygen) → produces water; hydrogen burns in air over a wide range, about 4–75% by volume.

24-005.r: Least polluting fuel → hydrogen (burns to water); coal, kerosene and diesel are fossil fuels giving carbon dioxide and harmful gases.

24-006.r: Hydrogen stored physically → compressed gas in high-pressure cylinders (350–700 bar), or as liquid.

24-007.r: Heavy water (D2O, deuterium oxide) → both moderator and coolant in nuclear reactors: slows neutrons well and rarely absorbs them.

24-014.r: Heavy water and deuterium → discovered by Harold C. Urey, American physical chemist; Chemistry Nobel 1934.

24-015.r: Heavy water (D2O) → molecular weight about 20; ordinary water about 18, as deuterium is twice as heavy as ordinary hydrogen.

24-016.r: Hard water (calcium and magnesium sulphates, chlorides) → unfit for drinking, washing with soap (scum), boilers (deposits) and irrigation: all four. These salts cause permanent hardness.

24-018.r: Pure water → pH 7 (neutral); below 7 acidic, above 7 basic (alkaline).

24-020.r: Book's answer: rainwater is the purest form of water, as water on Earth mixes with acidic and alkaline minerals.
24-020.c: Distilled water is normally taken as the purest form; rainwater picks up dissolved gases and dust. Rainwater is purest only among natural waters, so (d) is the better answer here.

24-021.r: Water dissolves ionic salts well → it is polar (dipolar) with a high dipole moment and hydrates ions like Na+ and Cl–.

24-023.r: Large-scale drinking water from saline water → desalination (removing salts and minerals); used for drinking, irrigation, industry.

24-024.r: Chlorine → used to purify drinking water (kills bacteria and microbes); also in swimming pools and bleach.

24-025.r: Sea water → pure water by reverse osmosis (RO): pressure forces water through a semipermeable membrane, leaving salts behind; main large-scale desalination method.

24-027.r: Alum (aluminium sulphate) cleans muddy water by coagulation: fine charged particles clump into heavy clusters and settle.

24-028.r: Vanaspati ghee → hydrogenation: hydrogen passed through vegetable oil at 8–10 atmospheres and 150–180°C with nickel (Ni) catalyst.

25-001.r: Noble gases (Group 18) → odourless, colourless, monatomic, very low reactivity: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon. Actinium is not a noble gas.

25-003.r: Air by volume: nitrogen about 78% (78–79%), oxygen 20.95%, argon 0.93%, carbon dioxide about 0.03% (lowest here).

25-005.r: Lighter than air (molar mass below about 28.97 g/mol) → helium (4.0 g/mol). Hydrogen chloride (36.5) and sulfur dioxide (64) are heavier.

25-006.r: Gaseous cycles (reservoir: air or ocean) → nitrogen, oxygen, carbon, water; sedimentary cycles (crust) → iron, calcium, phosphorus, sulfur. Hydrogen is not counted.

25-007.r: Deep-sea divers breathe oxygen + helium ('Heliox'): helium lowers airway resistance and, being poorly soluble, does not enter blood under pressure like nitrogen.

25-010.r: Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) → octahedral shape: six fluorine atoms around a central sulfur atom.

25-011.r: Ammonia → easily soluble in water, as both are polar molecules that form hydrogen bonds.

25-012.r: Laughing gas → nitrous oxide (N2O): colourless, causes euphoria; used as anaesthetic and sedative in medical and dental work.
25-012.t: Nitrous oxide (N2O), not nitric oxide (NO) or nitrogen dioxide.

25-017.r: 'Stranger gas' → xenon (Xe, atomic number 54), noble gas of Group 18; about 0.08 parts per million of air; discovered by William Ramsay.

25-018.r: Nitrous oxide (N2O), not nitric oxide (NO), is laughing gas. True: Bordeaux mixture (copper sulphate + calcium hydroxide) is a fungicide; boric acid preserves food; dry ice = solid CO2.

25-019.r: Nitrogen cycle: fixation, ammonification, nitrification, denitrification (bacteria turn nitrate/nitrite into nitrogen). Its discharge keeps nitrogen in lithosphere and atmosphere unchanged.

25-020.r: Permanent gas (thought incapable of liquefaction under normal conditions) → nitrogen, about 78% of air; others: hydrogen, carbon monoxide.

25-021.r: Aircraft tyres → filled with nitrogen: it does not support combustion, preventing wheel fires on hot landings; lowest-cost such gas.

25-022.r: Insectivorous plants trap and digest insects → to make up for nitrogen deficiency.

25-023.r: Insectivorous plants (Nepenthes, Dionaea, Drosera, Utricularia) → grow in waterlogged, nitrogen-deficient soil and take nitrogen from insects.

25-024.r: Gas balloons → usually filled with helium: lighter than air, inert, does not form an explosive mixture with air.

25-025.r: Helium is preferred to hydrogen in balloons → it is inert and does not form an explosive mixture with air; hydrogen is highly flammable.
25-025.t: The reason is safety, not lower density: hydrogen is lighter than helium.

25-026.r: Tear gas (book's answer: chlorine, used as a reagent to make it) → agents like alpha-chloroacetophenone, 2-chlorobenzalmalononitrile, acrolein; cause tears and pain.

25-028.r: Foul smell of dead fish → amino compounds, mainly trimethylamine (a tertiary amine).

25-029.r: Iodine → solid (bluish-black, lustrous) at normal temperature. Halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine) have 7 outer electrons.

25-030.r: Most reactive halogen → fluorine, the smallest atom. Halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine; also tennessine, 117) form Group 17.
